authoring.value:
Along $C$, $x(t)=1$, $y(t)=t$, and $z(t)=t^2$, so $x'(t)=0$, $y'(t)=1$, and $z'(t)=2t$. Substitute both the coordinates and their derivatives:

$$\int_C 2y\,dx+\ln x\,dy+3z\,dz
=\int_1^3\left(2t\cdot0+\ln(1)\cdot1+3t^2\cdot2t\right)\,dt
=\int_1^3 6t^3\,dt.$$

Thus the equivalent integral is $\int_1^3 6t^3\,dt$, and its value is $[\tfrac32t^4]_1^3=120$.

The original source accepted $\int_1^3 6t^2\,dt$ and its worked solution changed $3t^2\cdot2t$ into $6t^2$. That simplification loses a factor of $t$. The study choice replaces that exponent with $3$; all other original choices are retained.

decisions.question: e-7118

source.question: e-7118
source.value:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) = t, \qquad
y(t) = t^2.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+y)\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(({x}^{2}+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+{t}^{2})\cdot 1+t\cdot 2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{t}^{2}+2{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

decisions.question: e-9517

source.question: e-9517
source.value:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) =2t, \qquad 
y(t) = \cos t , \qquad 
z(t) = \sin t.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =2\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2t)^{3}\cdot (2)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

decisions.question: e-9528

source.question: e-9528
source.value:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) = \cos t, \qquad
y(t) = 3\sin t.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt-x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-3{sin}^{2}⁡t-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,dt \\  & =-3{t|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-3\pi \end{aligned}
$$
